items.definition: the part of your email account where new messages arrive
exampleSentences: She checks her inbox first thing every morning.
By Friday, his inbox had over two hundred unread messages.

items.definition: a file, such as a document or photo, that is sent together with an email
exampleSentences: Please find the report as an attachment.
The attachment was too large to send, so she used a shared link.

items.definition: the person who receives a letter, email, or package
exampleSentences: Make sure the recipient's address is correct before you click send.
The message had three recipients in the 'To' field.

items.definition: the person who sends a letter, email, or package
exampleSentences: The email looked strange, so she checked the sender's address carefully.
Always check who the sender is before opening an unexpected attachment.

items.definition: to send an email or message that you received on to another person
exampleSentences: Could you forward me the invoice from last week?
He forwarded the supplier's email to the whole team.

items.definition: to send an email reply to everyone who received the original message, not just the sender
exampleSentences: Only use reply all when everyone on the list really needs to see your answer.
She accidentally hit reply all and sent her joke to the whole department.

items.definition: the short line of text at the top of an email that says what the message is about
exampleSentences: Always write a clear subject line so the reader knows what to expect.
Her subject line simply said, 'Quick question about Thursday.'

items.definition: a version of a piece of writing that is not yet finished
exampleSentences: He saved the email as a draft and finished it the next morning.
Can you read this draft before I send it to the whole team?

items.definition: a short block of text at the end of an email that gives your name and contact details
exampleSentences: Her email signature includes her job title and phone number.
Add a signature so people know how to reach you.

items.definition: a series of connected emails on the same subject
exampleSentences: I lost track of who said what in that long email thread.
Please keep replying in the same thread so we have one record.

items.definition: letters, emails, or messages that people send to each other, especially for business
exampleSentences: All correspondence with the supplier should be copied to the finance team.
She keeps a folder for important business correspondence.

items.definition: to let someone know that you have received their message or request
exampleSentences: Please acknowledge this email so I know it arrived safely.
He acknowledged her request within an hour.

items.definition: to say that something is true or that it will definitely happen
exampleSentences: Could you confirm the time of tomorrow's call?
She confirmed that the documents had been sent.

items.definition: to attach something to a letter or email, or put it inside an envelope
exampleSentences: I have enclosed a copy of the invoice for your records.
Please find enclosed the signed contract.

items.definition: to reply to a letter, email, or question
exampleSentences: He usually responds to emails within a day.
She hasn't responded to my message yet.

items.definition: to say sorry for something you did wrong
exampleSentences: She apologized for the delay in her reply.
We apologize for any inconvenience this may cause.

items.definition: a request for information
exampleSentences: Thank you for your inquiry about our new service.
We received several inquiries after the announcement.

items.definition: to explain something more clearly so that it is easier to understand
exampleSentences: Could you clarify what you mean by 'as soon as possible'?
He wrote back to clarify the delivery date.

items.definition: to officially tell someone about something
exampleSentences: We will notify you as soon as the order ships.
Please notify us if your address changes.

items.definition: polite and respectful in a formal way
exampleSentences: Even when complaining, keep your email courteous.
Thank you for your courteous reply to my complaint.

items.definition: done quickly and without delay
exampleSentences: Thank you for your prompt reply to my question.
We appreciate a prompt response whenever possible.

items.definition: giving only the necessary information, in a few clear words
exampleSentences: Keep your emails concise so people actually read them.
Her message was concise and easy to follow.

items.definition: serious and correct in style, suitable for official situations or for people you do not know well
exampleSentences: Use a formal tone when you write to someone you do not know well.
The email was too formal for a message to a close colleague.

items.definition: relaxed and friendly in style, suitable for people you know well
exampleSentences: You can be more informal when you email a close colleague.
His informal style surprised the new intern.

items.definition: a short phrase at the end of an email or letter, before your name, such as 'Best regards'
exampleSentences: She ended the email with a warm sign-off.
'Best,' is a common sign-off in casual business emails.

items.definition: needing attention or action very soon
exampleSentences: Mark the email as urgent if you need a same-day reply.
This is urgent: the shipment leaves in an hour.

items.definition: a message that helps someone remember to do something
exampleSentences: I sent a reminder because she hadn't replied.
The system sends an automatic reminder two days before the due date.

items.definition: to carefully check a piece of writing for mistakes before sending it
exampleSentences: Always proofread an important email before you hit send.
She proofread the message twice and still found a typo.

items.definition: a small mistake made when typing, such as a misspelled word
exampleSentences: There's a typo in the second sentence.
He noticed the typo just after clicking send.

items.definition: to pass a problem to someone with more authority because it has not been solved
exampleSentences: If you don't hear back in two days, escalate the issue to the manager.
She escalated her complaint after three unanswered emails.

lessons.title: Grammar: Polite requests and indirect questions

items.definition: how to make requests and ask questions more politely in business emails
items.explanationTR:
In business emails, direct questions and commands can sound demanding. Polite requests and indirect questions soften the tone.

• Common polite requests use a modal plus a softener:
  - Could you send me the file by Friday?
  - Would you mind checking this again?
  - I would appreciate it if you could confirm the date.

• Indirect questions hide a normal question inside a longer sentence. After the connecting word (if, whether, when, why, what), the word order returns to statement order — subject before verb — and we drop 'do/does/did':
  - Direct: When is the report due?
  - Indirect: Could you tell me when the report is due?
  - Direct: Did you receive my message?
  - Indirect: I was wondering if you received my message.

• Useful openers: 'I was wondering if...', 'Could you tell me...', 'Do you know whether...', 'I'd like to know if...'

These forms make an email sound professional and considerate, especially when writing to people you do not know well or when asking for something that takes their time.

questions.prompt: I was wondering ---- the shipment will arrive.
questions.explanationTR: An indirect question keeps normal statement order, so 'when' alone connects the two clauses correctly: 'I was wondering when the shipment will arrive.' 'When will' repeats direct-question order, which is wrong inside an indirect question.

questions.prompt: Could you tell me ---- the invoice was sent?
questions.explanationTR: 'If' introduces an indirect yes/no question with normal statement order: 'Could you tell me if the invoice was sent?' 'Whether does' wrongly adds an extra auxiliary, and 'that if' incorrectly combines two connectors.

questions.prompt: ---- you mind forwarding me last week's report?
questions.explanationTR: 'Would you mind' is the fixed polite pattern for asking someone to do something. 'Will/Should/Must/Have you mind' are not natural English in this request.

questions.prompt: I would appreciate it ---- you could confirm receipt of this email.
questions.explanationTR: 'I would appreciate it if...' is the standard polite fixed phrase for a request. 'That', 'whether', and 'because' do not fit this fixed expression, and 'when' changes the meaning to a time reference.

questions.prompt: She was wondering ---- the new schedule had been sent to everyone.
questions.explanationTR: 'Whether' introduces the indirect question with normal statement order: 'whether the new schedule had been sent'. The other options add an extra auxiliary or connector that does not belong in an indirect question.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the most polite way to ask for a document?
options: Could you please send me the file when you have a moment?
You must send the file immediately.
questions.explanationTR: The polite modal 'could' plus 'please' and the softener 'when you have a moment' make this the most courteous option. The other sentences are direct commands or statements of want, which sound demanding in a business email.

questions.prompt: Do you know ---- the manager wants to move the call?
questions.explanationTR: 'Why' connects the indirect question with normal statement order: 'why the manager wants to move the call'. The other options add an unnecessary or misplaced auxiliary verb.

questions.prompt: I'd like to know ---- you have received my earlier email.
questions.explanationTR: 'If' alone correctly introduces the indirect question in statement order. The other options add an extra auxiliary ('did', 'does') or an unnecessary connector ('that'), which is not allowed in an indirect question.

items.definition: Eight short excerpts from business emails, each missing one key word

questions.prompt: I am writing with an ---- about your new pricing plans.
questions.explanationTR: After the article 'an', a singular noun is needed, so 'inquiry' fits. 'Inquiries' is plural, 'inquiring' and 'inquire' are verb forms, and 'inquest' is a different word meaning a legal investigation into a death.

questions.prompt: Please find ---- the signed contract for your records.
questions.explanationTR: 'Please find enclosed' is the standard fixed phrase for attaching a document to a letter or email. 'Enclose' and 'enclosing' are the wrong verb forms, 'enclosure' is a noun, and 'closed' is the wrong word entirely.

questions.prompt: Please accept my sincere ---- for the delay.
questions.explanationTR: After 'my sincere', a noun is needed, and 'apology' is the noun form. 'Apologize/apologized/apologizing' are verb forms, and 'apologetic' is an adjective, so none of them can follow 'my sincere'.

questions.prompt: Please mark your email as ---- if you need a reply today.
questions.explanationTR: After 'mark ... as', an adjective describes the noun, so 'urgent' is correct. 'Urgently' is an adverb, 'urgency' is a noun, and 'urge'/'urging' are verb forms, so none of them fit this position.

questions.prompt: Thank you for your ---- reply; it really helped us plan ahead.
questions.explanationTR: An adjective is needed before the noun 'reply', and 'prompt' is the adjective form. 'Promptly' is an adverb, 'promptness' is a noun, and 'prompts'/'prompted' are verb forms, so they cannot modify 'reply'.

questions.prompt: Could you ---- receipt of this email so I know it arrived?
questions.explanationTR: After the modal 'could', a verb must be in its base form, so 'acknowledge' is correct. The other options are a gerund, a past tense, a noun, and a third-person form, none of which can follow a modal verb.

questions.prompt: If the problem is not solved by Friday, I will have to ---- it to the regional manager.
questions.explanationTR: After 'have to', a verb must be in its base form, so 'escalate' (pass the problem to someone with more authority) is correct. 'Escalation' is a noun, and 'escalating', 'escalated' and 'escalates' are verb forms that cannot follow 'have to'.

questions.prompt: Sorry for the confusion — let me ---- what I meant in my last message.
questions.explanationTR: After 'let me', a verb must be in its base form, so 'clarify' is correct. 'Clarifying' and 'clarified' are wrong verb forms in this position, 'clarity' is a noun, and 'clarifies' is a third-person form.
